title: Emergency fleet guardrails and KPI surge retention sprint
creator: Jordan Patel
description:
Summary:
On 2026-03-12 we detected a sustained capacity shortfall across multiple Dedicated pools serving high-throughput customers. The incident manifested as request queuing, backpressure signals from the internal autoscaler, and SLA alerts for 3 major customers. Temporary mitigations preserved best-effort availability but increased latency and cost.

This ticket tracks the incident response work focused on: 1) short-term guardrails to preserve customer-facing KPIs, 2) experiments and code changes to eliminate the autoscale regression, and 3) consolidated post-incident action items that reduce recurrence risk.

Background:
- A change deployed as part of runtime-1.18 (kernel scheduling heuristics) altered the distribution of pod CPU/memory signals consumed by the fleet autoscaler. Under high-cardinality model routing (many model+route combos), our aggregator dropped transient token-counts causing the autoscaler to under-provision. Combined with a conservative backoff window introduced last year, pools failed to expand fast enough to meet burst demand.

Impact:
- 3 Dedicated customers experienced degraded throughput and elevated request latency for a 75-minute window. No data exfiltration. Financial SLA exposure estimated moderate (investigation ongoing).

Goals for this ticket:
- Ship emergency guardrails that reduce customer-visible impact for future shortfalls (rate-limited spillover, temporary headroom pools, targeted throttles for noisy routes).
- Fix the autoscale metric aggregation and roll out an A/B test comparing the previous heuristic vs corrected aggregator.
- Update runbooks and alerts to reduce mean-time-to-detect and mean-time-to-recover.

root_cause_summary: The fleet autoscaler relied on an online aggregation path that assumed idempotent updates across routing keys. A recent kernel scheduling change shifted emission timing (edge case of high-cardinality routing), producing transient zeroes that the aggregator interpreted as a true drop in demand. Combined with an overly aggressive backoff period, the autoscaler entered suppressed expansion mode during a legitimate demand spike.

risks_and_open_questions: Will automated headroom materially increase baseline cost? Need pricing impact analysis from Finance.
Are there other emission timing changes in recent releases that could surface similar mismatches? Runtime audit required.
How should we prioritize per-customer fallbacks vs global headroom when costs and latency trade off? Input required from Product.
Is more fine-grained per-route autoscaler state (vs aggregated pool view) necessary for long-term correctness?
